turns: Which hubs in the Midwest are most exposed to winter disruption?
results.answer: Minneapolis (MSP) is the most exposed Midwest hub for winter disruption, with a winter score of 48.2. That is moderate, not high. Chicago (39.9), Detroit (37.4) and Kansas City (33.8) are also moderate. Indianapolis (30.7) and Columbus (30.1) are low. MSP's main drivers are 146.4 freeze days/yr (min temp <= 0 C) and 20.4 days/yr with snowfall >= 1 cm. Chicago has 103.6 freeze days and 18.6 snow days. Detroit has 111.4 freeze days and 17.0 snow days. Chicago and Detroit are not a close call (2.5 points apart is not flagged for them, but Chicago's gap to Detroit is under 3 points, so treat their order as uncertain). Indianapolis and Columbus are a close call, so their order is not meaningful.

turns: Compare Miami and Houston in terms of hurricane and flood exposure.
results.answer: Miami is more exposed to hurricane and wind, and Houston is far more exposed to flood and heavy rain. On wind, Miami scores 51.9 (moderate) and Houston 43.1 (moderate). Miami's edge comes mostly from FEMA wind declarations (11 vs 8 over 20 years). Both see about 11 days/yr with gusts of 60 km/h or more (11.8 for Miami, 10.8 for Houston) and 0.2 days/yr at 90 km/h or more. On flood, Houston scores 74.7 (high) and Miami 32.4 (low). Houston has 23.6 days/yr with 25 mm or more of rain, against 9.2 for Miami. It has 4.2 days/yr at 50 mm or more, against 2.2. It also has 7 FEMA flood declarations, against 2 for Miami.

turns: What percentage of days in Denver last year had snowfall?
results.answer: In 2025, 10.1% of days in Denver had snowfall of at least 0.1 cm. That is 37 of 365 days. Days with at least 1 cm of snow were fewer: 17 days, or 4.7%.

turns: Why is the Dallas hub's weather disruption risk high?
results.answer: The premise is slightly off. Dallas's composite Weather Disruption Risk Score is 36.5, which is moderate, not high (high starts at 66). It does rank 2nd of 14 hubs, so it is high relative to the network but only moderate in absolute terms. Flood and heavy rain is the biggest contributor at 16.3 points. The drivers are 16.2 days/yr with at least 25 mm of rain and 3.6 days/yr with at least 50 mm. Next is wind at 9.9 points, led by 5 FEMA wind declarations over 20 years. Heat adds 6.8 points, from 54.6 days/yr at or above 35 C. Winter adds only 3.5 points.

turns: Rank the Midwest hubs by flood exposure.
And what about Chicago?
results.answer: Chicago (CHI) is 2nd of 6 Midwest hubs for flood exposure. Its flood score is 30.8, which is low and just under the moderate threshold of 33. Kansas City (MCI) is clearly ahead at 44.6, which is moderate. CHI is a close call with Minneapolis (MSP, 29.8), so their order is not meaningful. The main driver is 7 FEMA flood/severe storm declarations over 20 years (18.7 points), the most in the Midwest. Rain adds less: 5.8 days/yr with at least 25 mm and 0.4 days/yr with at least 50 mm. Chicago's flood score comes mostly from its declaration history, not from heavy rain. Its composite score is 25.9 (low, 7th of 14 in the network), and flood is its largest contributor at 9.2 points. In my previous answer I said CHI was also a close call with MCI's next hub. That was wrong. CHI is 13.8 points behind MCI. The close-call flags apply to CHI/MSP and MSP/CMH.

turns: Which three hubs have the highest overall weather disruption risk?
results.answer: The three highest composite scores are Houston (HOU) at 39.0, Dallas (DFW) at 36.5 and Newark (EWR) at 33.4. All three are rated moderate, and none is high. They rank highest relative to the other hubs, not in absolute terms. Houston's main drivers are 23.6 days/yr with at least 25 mm of rain and 8 FEMA wind declarations over 20 years. Dallas is driven by 16.2 days/yr of heavy rain and 54.6 days/yr above 35 C. Newark is driven by 7 FEMA wind declarations and 12.2 heavy-rain days/yr. Houston and Dallas are 2.5 points apart, which is within the 3-point close-call threshold, so their order is not meaningful. Dallas and Newark are 3.1 points apart, just outside that threshold. The tool flags Newark as a close call with the next hub, which was not retrieved, so its third place is uncertain.

turns: Which hubs face the biggest hurricane risk?
results.answer: Miami has the highest hurricane/high-wind score in the network at 51.9, which is moderate. Its main driver is 11 FEMA hurricane, tropical storm, tornado and wind declarations over 20 years, plus 11.8 days/yr with gusts of 60 km/h or more. Newark (43.3) and Houston (43.1) follow, then Dallas (39.6). All of these are moderate, and no hub reaches the high level. Newark and Houston are a close call, so their order is not meaningful. Atlanta (26.6) is low.

turns: Where is extreme heat the biggest problem for us?
results.answer: Phoenix is clearly the hub most exposed to extreme heat. Its heat score is 100 (high), driven by 137.4 days/yr with a max temperature of 35 C or more. Dallas is a distant second at 45.5 (moderate), with 54.6 days/yr above 35 C. Houston (22.3, 26.8 days/yr), Denver (14.8, 17.8 days/yr) and Kansas City (10.0, 12.0 days/yr) are all low. Heat is a real problem only at Phoenix and, to a moderate degree, at Dallas.

turns: Compare Denver, Minneapolis and Chicago for winter risk.
results.answer: Denver has the highest winter score of the three at 53.9, then Minneapolis at 48.2 and Chicago at 39.9. All three are only 'moderate' in absolute terms, and none is 'high' (66 or above). Denver has the most freeze days (152.2 days/yr at or below 0 C) and the most days with at least 1 cm of snow (22.4 days/yr). It also has 1 FEMA winter declaration. Minneapolis has 146.4 freeze days/yr and 20.4 snow days/yr, and no FEMA winter declarations. Chicago has 103.6 freeze days/yr, 18.6 snow days/yr and 0.6 heavy-snow days/yr, which is half the 1.2 days/yr at Denver and Minneapolis. On the composite score all three are 'low' and almost identical: Denver 27.1, Chicago 25.9, Minneapolis 25.8.

results.answer: Phoenix reached 35 C or more on 151 of the 366 days in 2024 (a leap year), which is 41.3% of the year. The data has no missing days.

turns: Why is Miami only moderate? It gets hurricanes all the time.
results.answer: Miami is #1 in the network for hurricane/wind risk, but that wind score is only 51.9, which is moderate. Miami's overall composite score is 22.7, which is low (rank 9 of 14). So Miami isn't "only moderate" overall. Its wind score is moderate, and its composite is lower still. The wind score has three parts. FEMA wind declarations are maxed out at 11 per 20 years, which gives 40 points. Gusts of 60 km/h or more occur on 11.8 days/yr (8.8 points). Gusts of 90 km/h or more occur on 0.2 days/yr (3.0 points). The 2021-2025 reanalysis data shows few damaging gusts, and the score is capped by fixed anchors. The composite also weights winter at 30%, flood at 30%, wind at 25% and heat at 15%. Miami scores about 0 on winter and heat, and its flood score is low (32.4). Wind adds only 13.0 composite points and flood adds 9.7.
